Bridged Self-Distillation for On-Policy Learning

Runsheng Chen, Yihong Liu, Raoyuan Zhao,Michael A. Hedderich, Hinrich Schütze, and Matthias Grabmair Email: {runsheng.chen, matthias.grabmair}@tum.de Email: {yihong, rzhao, hedderich}@cis.lmu.de Affiliation: Munich Center for Machine Learning (MCML) Affiliation: Technical University of Munich Affiliation: LMU Munich
Abstract

On-policy distillation can transfer the reasoning capabilities of a strong teacher to a smaller student. However, distillation from a stronger teacher model faces two mismatches: its solutions may be difficult for a smaller student to imitate, and its token-level probabilities may be incompatible with, or even unavailable to, the student. Existing methods handle these settings through different forms of supervision. To this end, we propose Bridged Self-Distillation (BSD), a unified framework for distilling from any teacher that provides reasoning traces. The model to be distilled from, termed the external teacher, first provides a reasoning trace as privileged context, which can be generated in an offline fashion. The student generates rollouts without this context, while a copy of the student conditioned on it, serving as the self-teacher, scores the same rollouts in the student’s own token space. BSD uses the resulting token-level guidance to adjust updates on unsuccessful rollouts, with a verifier providing the outcome signal. As the external teacher is queried only to produce text, the same training procedure applies to all teacher scenarios: shared-tokenizer, cross-tokenizer, and closed API teachers. Across these scenarios, BSD improves over the base model and outperforms baselines tailored to each scenario, offering a novel and unified pathway for distillation. Code is available: https://github.com/TUMLegalTech/Bridged-Self-Distillation

1 Introduction

Large reasoning models have become increasingly capable on tasks that require multi-step reasoning (Wei et al., 2022; Ahn et al., 2024; Muennighoff et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025). Much of this progress comes from post-training, typically including supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on reasoning traces and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) (Ouyang et al., 2022; Chung et al., 2024; Shao et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2025a; Ye et al., 2025b; Yu et al., 2025). Yet the cost of running a large reasoning model makes it desirable to transfer its capabilities to smaller student models that can respond more quickly and be deployed more widely (Hinton et al., 2015; Kim and Rush, 2016). On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as a promising post-training approach for this purpose, allowing a smaller model to learn from the guidance of a stronger teacher (Gu et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2024; Ko et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025; Lu and Lab, 2025; Li et al., 2026b; Song and Zheng, 2026).

In standard OPD, the student generates its own rollouts, and the teacher scores the student’s tokens to guide training (Ross et al., 2011; Agarwal et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026). This requires access to the teacher’s next-token distributions and a way to align them with the student’s tokenization. However, when teacher and student use different tokenizers, these distributions cannot be compared directly; when the teacher is available only through a closed API, they may be inaccessible. Cross-tokenizer OPD methods address the former by constructing mappings between the token spaces of the student and teacher (Zhang et al., 2024; Minixhofer et al., 2025; Boizard et al., 2025; Niu et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026), while black-box methods address the latter using feedback such as rubrics or sampled continuations (Jiang et al., 2023; Ye et al., 2026a; Fang et al., 2026; Xiong et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026). These methods expand the range of usable teachers, but require different training signals for different teacher settings (Figure 1, top). Alternatively, SFT can train on teacher-generated text without accessing probabilities, although directly imitating a much stronger model’s reasoning can be difficult for a small student (Zhang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026; Lyu et al., 2026). This motivates a unified on-policy learning method that can distill from any teacher capable of providing reasoning traces.

We propose Bridged Self-Distillation (BSD) to turn the reasoning of an external teacher into guidance on the student’s own rollouts (Figure 1, bottom). The external teacher is the model we aim to distill from, and BSD requires only its reasoning trace. Instead of training the student to imitate the teacher’s solution, as in SFT, we provide that solution as privileged context to a copy of the student. Inspired by on-policy self-distillation (Zhao et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a), this conditioned copy serves as a self-teacher, scoring rollouts generated by the student without the privileged context. Both versions score the same tokens in the student’s own token space, and the differences show how access to the teacher’s reasoning changes the student’s predictions along its rollouts. BSD uses these differences to adjust token-level penalties on unsuccessful rollouts, while a verifier determines the direction of the updates. Because the external teacher provides only text, the same training procedure applies to shared-tokenizer, cross-tokenizer, and closed API teachers.

We evaluate BSD under three forms of teacher access: (1) shared-tokenizer, (2) cross-tokenizer, and (3) closed API teachers. Across twelve teacher–student pairs and three math reasoning benchmarks, BSD remains effective in all three settings while avoiding the severe degradation that SFT exhibits in several pairs. Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We introduce BSD, a unified on-policy distillation framework that turns reasoning traces from external teachers into token-level guidance through a privileged self-teacher.

  • •

    We evaluate BSD across twelve teacher–student pairs spanning shared-tokenizer, cross-tokenizer, and closed API teachers, demonstrating that BSD generally outperforms the baselines across all three settings.

  • •

    Our analyses show that BSD maintains stable training, benefits from more complete reasoning traces, and concentrates its guidance on uncertain tokens, with stronger guidance associated with larger performance gains.

2 Preliminaries

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).

Let πθ\pi_{\theta} denote the policy model being optimized. For a question xx, the policy samples a group of rollouts {y(i)}i=1G\{y^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{G}, and a verifier assigns each rollout a binary reward r(i)∈{0,1}r^{(i)}\in\{0,1\}. GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) normalizes these rewards within the group:

A(i)=r(i)−mean⁡({r(j)}j=1G)std⁡({r(j)}j=1G),A^{(i)}\;=\;\frac{r^{(i)}-\operatorname{mean}\big(\{r^{(j)}\}_{j=1}^{G}\big)}{\operatorname{std}\big(\{r^{(j)}\}_{j=1}^{G}\big)}, (1)

and applies the advantage A(i)A^{(i)} uniformly to every token of y(i)y^{(i)} in a clipped policy-gradient update. When a group contains both outcomes, successful rollouts have positive advantage and unsuccessful rollouts have negative advantage. If all rollouts have the same outcome, their advantages are zero, and the group contributes no gradient. We omit the rollout index ii when considering a single rollout.

Privileged self-distillation. A privileged context zz is available during training but absent when the model generates rollouts or performs inference. In on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) (Zhao et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026), the model generates on-policy rollouts without zz as the student. A copy conditioned on zz acts as the teacher and scores the same tokens. RLSD (Yang et al., 2026a) uses the ratio of these two token probabilities to refine the rollout-level advantage at each token:

ut\displaystyle u_{t} =[πθ​(yt∣x,z,y<t)πθ​(yt∣x,y<t)]sign⁡(A),\displaystyle=\left[\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,z,y_{<t})}{\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}\right]^{\sign(A)}, (2)
A^tRLSD\displaystyle\hat{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{RLSD}} =A⁡[(1−λ)+λ​clip1±ϵ⁡(ut)].\displaystyle=A\big[(1-\lambda)+\lambda\,\clip_{1\pm\epsilon}\!\left(u_{t}\right)\big].

Here, clip1±ϵ⁡(⋅)\clip_{1\pm\epsilon}\!\left(\cdot\right) clips its argument to [1−ϵ,1+ϵ][1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon], and λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1] controls the strength of token-level reweighting. Because the multiplier is positive, reweighting preserves the sign of AA. Intuitively, in RLSD, the verifier determines the direction of the update while the privileged context changes how strongly individual tokens are updated.

3 Bridged Self-Distillation

To distill from teacher models with different tokenizers or text-only access, we need guidance that does not depend on their token probabilities. Directly imitating a stronger teacher’s reasoning can also be difficult for a smaller student. We therefore propose Bridged Self-Distillation (BSD), which only needs a teacher’s reasoning trace and turns it into guidance on the student’s own rollouts (Figure 2). We describe the key components below.

3.1 External Teacher

We refer to the model that we want to distill from as the external teacher. Given a question xx, it provides a reasoning trace zz, the text it returns when solving xx, which contains its full reasoning when this is exposed and only its final response otherwise. BSD uses zz as the privileged context for the self-teacher. Because the external teacher only needs to provide text, this setup applies to all scenarios, including shared-tokenizer, cross-tokenizer, and closed API teachers.

3.2 Self-Teacher

To turn zz into guidance on the student’s own reasoning, the student first generates a rollout yy from xx without zz. For each generated token yty_{t}, the student assigns the probability pt=πθ​(yt∣x,y<t)p_{t}=\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t}).

The self-teacher is a frozen copy πθ¯\pi_{\bar{\theta}} of the student conditioned on both xx and zz. Rather than generating a separate solution, the self-teacher scores the same rollout yy token by token, assigning qt=πθ¯​(yt∣x,z,y<t)q_{t}=\pi_{\bar{\theta}}(y_{t}\mid x,z,y_{<t}). As the two scores come from the same model and share the same token space, neither logits from the external teacher nor vocabulary alignment is needed.

We define the token-level guidance as their per-token log-probability difference:

δt=sg⁡[log⁡qt−log⁡pt],\delta_{t}\;=\;\sg\big[\log q_{t}-\log p_{t}\big], (3)

where sg⁡[⋅]\sg[\cdot] denotes the stop-gradient operator. A positive δt\delta_{t} means the self-teacher assigns more probability to the student’s chosen token after reading zz; a negative value means it assigns less.

3.3 Learning

The self-teacher provides token-level guidance, while a verifier checks whether each rollout reaches the correct answer. GRPO converts these outcomes into the group-relative advantage AA (Eq. 1). For an unsuccessful rollout with A<0A<0, BSD instead uses the guidance δt\delta_{t} to set a token-specific weight:

wt=(1−λ)+λ​clip1±ϵ⁡(e−δt).w_{t}\;=\;(1-\lambda)+\lambda\,\clip_{1\pm\epsilon}\!\left(e^{-\delta_{t}}\right). (4)

When δt<0\delta_{t}<0, the self-teacher assigns less probability to the chosen token, so wt>1w_{t}>1 and that token receives a stronger penalty. When δt>0\delta_{t}>0, the penalty is reduced. The coefficient λ\lambda controls the strength of this reweighting, which decays over training, while clipping bounds its effect.

The weight wtw_{t} is applied only to unsuccessful rollouts, while the successful ones are unchanged:

A~t={A​wtif ​A<0,Aotherwise.\tilde{A}_{t}\;=\;\begin{cases}A\,w_{t}&\text{if }A<0,\\ A&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} (5)

This means that successful rollouts retain their advantage, as in GRPO, allowing the student to reinforce correct solutions it found without the external teacher’s guidance. Because wtw_{t} is positive, the token-level guidance changes the magnitude of a penalty without changing the sign of AA.

The student model is then optimized by maximizing the following policy-gradient objective 𝒥⁡(θ)=𝔼⁡[∑tA~t​log⁡πθ​(yt∣x,y<t)]\mathcal{J}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\big[\sum_{t}\tilde{A}_{t}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})\big].11 1 BSD coincides with GRPO on successful rollouts and, to first order, adds an OPD-style correction on unsuccessful rollouts; see Proposition 1 in Appendix C.

4 Experimental Setup

4.1 Models

Backbone models. We use three Qwen3 models as the student models (Yang et al., 2025) (in thinking mode): Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-1.7B, and Qwen3-4B. We also use Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as an additional backbone, which we first fine-tune on 1,000 reasoning traces to enable it to produce reasoning blocks. We refer to the fine-tuned model as Qwen3-4B-Instruct and use it as another student.

Teacher models. We consider three models as external teachers with different access settings: Qwen3-32B (Yang et al., 2025) as a shared-tokenizer teacher, Nemotron-3-30B-A3B (NVIDIA et al., 2025) as a cross-tokenizer teacher, and GPT-5.6 Luna (OpenAI, 2026) as a closed API teacher.

4.2 Training

Data. We use the mathematical reasoning subset of OpenThoughts (Guha et al., 2026). For each teacher–student pair, we sample 2,400 training problems, and the external teacher provides one reasoning trace zz per problem. The traces of Qwen3-32B and Nemotron-3-30B-A3B average about 4,000 tokens, while GPT-5.6 Luna returns only its final response, which averages 247 tokens.

Implementation details. We implement BSD using verl (Sheng et al., 2025) and vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023). Each student model is trained for 150 updates on NVIDIA H100/H200 GPUs. Further details are provided in Appendix A.

4.3 Evaluation

Benchmarks. We evaluate on three competition-level mathematics benchmarks: AIME 2024 (Mathematical Association of America, 2024), AIME 2025 (Mathematical Association of America, 2025), and HMMT 2025 (Dekoninck et al., 2026). We select the best checkpoints using a separate set of 128 development problems from OpenThoughts.

Metrics. For each benchmark problem, we generate four samples. We report Avg@4, the average correctness of the four samples, in Table 1, and Pass@4, the proportion of problems solved by at least one sample, in Table 14. The evaluation settings, the teachers’ own scores, and the selected checkpoints are in Appendices A and F.

4.4 Baselines

We consider the following baselines, which use the same backbones and training problems as BSD.

Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). We train each student to imitate the external teacher’s reasoning traces (Kim and Rush, 2016) using the same traces that serve as privileged context for BSD.

Vanilla OPD. For the shared-tokenizer teacher, we use standard OPD (Lu and Lab, 2025), which is optimized by minimizing the log-probability differences between student and teacher.

Cross-Tokenizer OPD (xOPD). For the cross-tokenizer teacher, we use cross-tokenizer OPD (Niu et al., 2026), denoted xOPD, which aligns the two tokenizations and maps teacher token log-probabilities onto student tokens.

Rubric-Based OPD (ROPD). For the closed API teacher, we use ROPD (Fang et al., 2026), which asks the teacher to derive a rubric for each question and score the student’s rollouts against it.

5 Main Results

We examine how BSD performs under different forms of teacher access. Across twelve teacher–student pairs, we first compare BSD with SFT and the OPD baseline designed for each of the shared-tokenizer, cross-tokenizer, and closed API settings. We then track performance and response length throughout training to examine how BSD and the baselines affect the student’s behavior.

5.1 Comparing Teacher Access

BSD consistently improves over the base model and outperforms the distillation baselines across teacher settings. Table 1 reports Avg@4 for four students paired with shared-tokenizer, cross-tokenizer, and closed API teachers. BSD improves over the base model in all twelve teacher–student pairs, with gains of 1.2 to 4.7 points, and achieves the best average score in eleven pairs.

Shared-tokenizer teacher. Qwen3-32B shares the students’ tokenizer, allowing vanilla OPD to score their rollouts directly with teacher token probabilities. BSD outperforms SFT for all four students by 3.3 to 8.6 points in average score, while SFT falls below the base model for three of them. Thus, even within the same model family, directly imitating a much stronger teacher’s reasoning can be difficult for smaller students (Zhang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025). BSD also matches or outperforms vanilla OPD for every student: the two tie in average score for Qwen3-1.7B, and BSD scores up to 3.6 points higher for the other three. This indicates that sharing a tokenizer does not ensure compatible reasoning patterns between distinct models, which prior work identifies as important for successful OPD (Li et al., 2026b). BSD instead uses a self-teacher, a copy of the student conditioned on the external teacher’s reasoning, so that the token-level guidance comes from the student’s own model and is therefore more compatible.

Cross-tokenizer teacher. Because the teacher model Nemotron-3-30B-A3B uses a different tokenizer from the students, xOPD must align the two tokenizations and map the teacher’s token probabilities onto the student’s tokens. Nevertheless, xOPD does not yield consistent gains over the base models. It improves the average score of Qwen3-0.6B by 3.4 points, but brings only marginal gains of 0.5 and 0.6 points for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-4B-Instruct, respectively, and decreases the score of Qwen3-1.7B by 0.8 points. This indicates that constructing a mapping makes cross-tokenizer OPD possible, but does not guarantee effective token-level supervision. In contrast, BSD improves all four base models by 1.2 to 4.4 points and outperforms xOPD for three of the four students, with Qwen3-0.6B as the only exception. BSD therefore provides a strong alternative for cross-tokenizer distillation, obtaining guidance directly in the student’s token space without mappings between distinct vocabularies.

Closed API teacher. GPT-5.6 Luna is accessible only through a text API and exposes neither token probabilities nor its tokenizer. Moreover, it returns short final responses averaging 247 tokens, compared with about 4,000 tokens from the other two teachers. Directly using these responses as SFT targets causes the students to imitate their length (cf. Section 5.2). Consequently, SFT falls below the base model for three of the four students, with Qwen3-0.6B dropping from 10.8 to 2.8. ROPD handles the lack of token probabilities by asking the external teacher to derive a rubric and score student rollouts during training. BSD outperforms SFT for all four students by 3.1 to 9.7 points and ROPD by 0.6 to 3.6 points. BSD achieves these gains by using each API response as privileged context for the self-teacher while allowing the student to generate its own rollouts, without training the student to reproduce their form.

5.2 Training Progression

We further examine how distillation changes the students throughout training. Figure 3 tracks two aspects of this progression: response length across all twelve teacher--student pairs and benchmark performance in a representative closed API setting.22 2 More performance curves for other teacher–student pairs are provided in Appendix H, where SFT performance also frequently deteriorates over training.

Response length. Figure 3a–c shows that the effect of SFT on response length depends strongly on the external teacher. With the shared-tokenizer teacher, response lengths remain largely stable for all methods. With the cross-tokenizer teacher, BSD and xOPD remain stable, whereas SFT usually increases the response lengths, most notably for Qwen3-1.7B. The most pronounced shift occurs with the closed API teacher, whose responses average only 247 tokens. SFT trains directly on these short responses, causing all four students to gradually shorten their outputs. In contrast, BSD and the corresponding OPD baselines maintain relatively stable response lengths across all twelve pairs. These trends show that using the external teacher’s reasoning trace as privileged context allows BSD to preserve the student’s output form without forcing it to reproduce the trace’s length.

Performance. A substantial decline in performance accompanies the response-length drift under the closed API teacher. Figure 3d illustrates this behavior for Qwen3-4B-Instruct distilled from GPT-5.6 Luna. SFT is already below the base model at the beginning, and its performance falls to nearly zero by the end of training. The additional curves in Appendix H show similar collapses or declines of SFT in other teacher–student pairs. These results further indicate that directly imitating a stronger teacher’s reasoning traces can lead to unstable training. In contrast, ROPD and BSD maintain stable or slightly improving performance throughout training. BSD is particularly notable because it uses the same external-teacher reasoning traces as SFT, but treats them as privileged context to guide the student’s own rollouts rather than as targets to imitate. Appendix I further shows that SFT suffers from catastrophic forgetting on two out-of-domain benchmarks, whereas BSD does not.

6 Further Analysis

6.1 Ablation Study

BSD combines privileged context from an external teacher with verifier-guided learning and applies token-level guidance only to unsuccessful rollouts. We ablate these design choices by asking three questions: (1) whether privileged context itself improves learning, (2) how much reasoning the context should contain, and (3) whether the verifier and the restriction to unsuccessful rollouts are needed. We study these questions in the shared-tokenizer setting using Qwen3-4B as the student and Qwen3-32B as the external teacher. All variants use the same training problems and optimization setup.

BSD-trace, which uses the full reasoning trace as in the main experiments, serves as the reference. For (1), we compare it with GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), which has no privileged context or self-teacher, and RLSD (Yang et al., 2026a), which uses only the ground-truth answer while otherwise following BSD. For (2), BSD-hint uses a three-sentence hint and BSD-guide uses up to eight reasoning steps without computations, both followed by the answer and derived from the full trace (obtained by using the prompts in Appendix B). For (3), BSD (w/ succ.) additionally weights successful rollouts, while OPSD (Zhao et al., 2026) uses the self-teacher’s token-level signal on every rollout without a verifier. Figure 4 reports training accuracy in panels (a)–(b) and Avg@4 in panel (c).

Privileged context facilitates reinforcement learning. GRPO, RLSD, and BSD-trace exhibit nearly identical training-accuracy curves, with their average differences remaining below 0.2, although BSD-trace shows a slight advantage in the middle of training (Figure 4a). Nevertheless, Avg@4 increases from 59.2 for the base model to 60.6 with GRPO, 61.7 with answer-conditioned RLSD, and 63.9 with trace-conditioned BSD. Privileged context therefore improves how verifier feedback transfers to downstream problems.

More complete reasoning produces stronger gains. Changing the privileged context from a short hint to a full trace has little effect on the training dynamics, as the three variants follow similar accuracy curves (Figure 4b). However, BSD-hint scores 61.7, while BSD-guide reaches 62.5 and BSD-trace further improves to 63.9 (Figure 4c), indicating that downstream performance benefits from more detailed reasoning in the privileged context.

The verifier and the restriction to unsuccessful rollouts matter. BSD (w/ succ.) scores 61.4, below the 63.9 of BSD-trace, so extending the weight to successful rollouts does not help (Figure 4c). OPSD scores 59.7 and declines over training, from 63.3 at step 25 to 55.8 at step 150, while its responses on the benchmarks shorten from 16.8k to 12.5k tokens (Appendix D). The other variants keep the response length of the base model.

6.2 What the Token-Level Guidance Captures

BSD uses the token-level guidance δt\delta_{t} to distribute verifier feedback across the tokens of an unsuccessful rollout. To understand this signal, we examine which tokens it emphasizes, whether its strength is associated with BSD’s gains, and how it affects the student’s behavior. Table 2 reports the quantitative results averaged across teachers, with the measurement setup described in Appendix A, while Figure 5 illustrates a concrete example.

Guidance targets uncertain tokens and tracks performance gains. The correlation ρH\rho_{H} between per-token guidance magnitude and the student’s token entropy on unsuccessful rollouts ranges from 0.830.83 to 0.900.90, indicating that the strongest guidance concentrates on tokens where the student is most uncertain. Its magnitude also follows the gains: Qwen3-4B-Instruct has both the weakest guidance and the smallest gain, whereas Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B receive stronger guidance and achieve larger gains. Thus, BSD achieves larger gains when the privileged context more strongly changes the student’s predictions, particularly at uncertain tokens.

Case study: BSD encourages self-correction. Figure 5 shows an AIME24 problem where the base Qwen3-4B finds the correct integer N=5694N=5694 but misreads its quotient and remainder when it is divided by 10001000. Given the same prefix containing this mistake, the base model continues without revisiting the division, whereas the student trained with BSD re-checks the step, identifies the error, and reaches the correct answer. Across eight continuations from this prefix, the BSD student solves the problem six times, compared with four for the base model. This example illustrates how BSD can help the student revisit and correct an uncertain intermediate step rather than persist with an initially plausible but incorrect rollout.33 3 Appendix E further compares the wording of responses from the base model and the BSD-trained student, and Appendix D shows an example of the token-level guidance under the trace and under the answer.

7 Related Work

Knowledge distillation. Knowledge distillation transfers supervision from a stronger teacher to a smaller student through output distributions or generated sequences (Hinton et al., 2015; Kim and Rush, 2016). For reasoning models, this idea is commonly instantiated by training on teacher-generated reasoning traces, although large teacher–student gaps can make direct imitation difficult (Shridhar et al., 2023; Hsieh et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2026; Lyu et al., 2026). On-policy distillation instead learns from student-generated rollouts under token-level teacher guidance (Gu et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026b). Recent variants extend OPD to heterogeneous tokenizers (Minixhofer et al., 2025; Boizard et al., 2025; Niu et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026) and black-box teachers (Ye et al., 2026a; Xiong et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026), but typically require setting-specific supervision. In contrast, BSD offers an effective and unified framework for all these settings.

Privileged information and self-distillation. Learning with privileged information provides a general framework for exploiting supervision that is available only during training, with generalized distillation connecting this idea to teacher–student learning (Vapnik and Vashist, 2009; Lopez-Paz et al., 2016). In language models, context distillation instantiates this principle by internalizing information from instructions, demonstrations, or other contextual signals into a model that later operates without them (Snell et al., 2022; Shin et al., 2025; Duan et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2026b). Recent self-distillation methods further use the model itself as a privileged teacher by conditioning it on answers, solutions, feedback, or successful trajectories (Zhao et al., 2026; Penaloza et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026b; Ding, 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a; Pan et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a; Kim et al., 2026). BSD follows this privileged paradigm, but uses reasoning from an external teacher as the privileged context.

8 Conclusion

We introduced BSD, a unified framework for distilling from any teacher that provides reasoning traces. BSD uses the external teacher’s reasoning trace as privileged context for a self-teacher, producing compatible token-level guidance in the student’s own token space without teacher probabilities or vocabulary mappings. Across twelve teacher–student pairs spanning shared-tokenizer, cross-tokenizer, and closed API settings, BSD improves every base model and achieves the best or tied average performance among the distillation methods in eleven pairs. Our analyses further show that BSD supports stable training, benefits from more complete reasoning, and focuses its guidance on uncertain tokens, establishing reasoning traces as a common and effective interface for on-policy distillation.

Limitations

We evaluate BSD with shared-tokenizer, cross-tokenizer, and closed API teachers across twelve teacher–student pairs and analyze its token-level guidance. However, we acknowledge three main limitations.

First, due to computational constraints, our experiments are limited to students of up to 4B parameters from one model family and to English competition mathematics. Future work could examine whether the gains of BSD hold for larger students, other model families, and other domains.

Second, BSD relies on a verifier to set the direction of each update, so it applies only to tasks whose answers can be checked automatically and not to open-ended ones. Whether the agreement between the student and the external teacher can serve as a verifier in such tasks remains to be explored.

Finally, our analysis relates the token-level guidance to the gains of BSD only through correlations across students. It characterizes where the guidance concentrates but does not establish which tokens it helps, or why, which we leave for future work.

Ethics Statement

This work fine-tunes publicly released language models on publicly available mathematical reasoning datasets and evaluates them with automatic verifiers. It involves no human subjects, no personally identifiable information, and no newly collected data. The method transfers reasoning capability that the teacher models already expose through their public interfaces, so we do not identify risks beyond those general to improving open-weight reasoning models.

The closed API teacher is queried through its official API solely to obtain responses for non-commercial research. The students trained with these responses serve only to study distillation methods: we do not deploy them, offer them as a service, or use them to develop models that compete with the API provider. We release only code, and release no model weights and no datasets, including the teacher’s reasoning traces.

Use of AI Assistants. The authors used AI assistants for code development, the organization of experiments and analyses, figure preparation, and manuscript drafting and language editing. All reported experimental results and scientific interpretations were reviewed by the authors, who take responsibility for the final paper.

Appendix A Experimental Details

Teacher traces.

Teacher traces are generated once, before training, with the settings in Table 3 and the prompts in Appendix B. For a closed teacher that hides its reasoning, the trace is built from the response it returns: we enclose the derivation of the response in a reasoning block (<think> and </think>) and place its boxed final answer after the block, which is the format of the students’ own responses. Within a teacher–student pair, BSD and SFT use the same traces, BSD as privileged context for the self-teacher and SFT as training targets.

Training.

Tables 4 and 5 give the training configuration. All methods train LoRA adapters (Hu et al., 2022), and the learning rate is warmed up linearly over the first 10 updates and is constant afterwards. Training sets are identical for all methods within a teacher–student pair. For BSD, the student’s score ptp_{t} uses its current log-probabilities, and the rollout–trainer gap is corrected with token-level truncated importance sampling (Yu et al., 2025). During training, BSD adds one forward pass of the self-teacher over the student’s rollouts. This pass takes 7 to 18 seconds per update, depending on the length of the trace, which is under 10% of the update time. The limit of 2,048 tokens on the prompt applies to the student’s prompt, which contains only the question. The self-teacher’s prompt also contains the trace and has a separate limit of 12,288 tokens. The longest question and trace together take 8,950 tokens, so no trace is truncated in any run; the hint and guide of Section 6.1 are shorter than the full trace.

Compute.

In total, the training, evaluation, and ablation runs reported in this paper take about 1,450 GPU-hours on NVIDIA H100 and H200 GPUs. Table 6 reports the GPU-hours of training with each method for the Qwen3-4B student, measured on NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The values cover the 150 updates and exclude checkpoint saving, checkpoint evaluation, and the generation of the teacher traces before training. OPD and xOPD keep the teacher on one additional GPU during training, which is counted, and ROPD queries the teacher through its API, whose compute is not counted.

Evaluation.

Table 7 gives the evaluation parameters. Checkpoints are selected on the development set, and the earliest checkpoint is taken in case of a tie. Each of the three benchmarks contains 30 problems. Final answers are checked with Math-Verify.44 4 https://github.com/huggingface/Math-Verify

Guidance measurement.

For Table 2, each student generates six rollouts for each of 24 hard problems shared by all students before training, and each rollout is scored under one verified trace from each of the three teachers. We write δ¯\bar{\delta} for the mean of the signed guidance δt\delta_{t} over all tokens of the unsuccessful rollouts, and Table 2 reports its absolute value |δ¯||\bar{\delta}|. The mean is negative for every teacher–student pair, so the self-teacher assigns on average a lower probability to the student’s tokens than the student does. This quantity differs from the mean absolute guidance |δ|¯\overline{|\delta|}, in which positive and negative values do not cancel; it is 0.163, 0.191, 0.202, and 0.110 for Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-4B-Instruct, respectively, so the last student has the smallest value under both statistics. The correlation ρH\rho_{H} is computed within each of the same rollouts and averaged over them.

Teacher evaluation.

Table 8 reports Avg@4 of the external teachers on the three benchmarks, with four samples per problem and seeds {0,1,2,3}\{0,1,2,3\}. Qwen3-32B and Nemotron-3-30B-A3B are evaluated under the students’ protocol: thinking enabled, temperature 1.0, top-p 1.0, and a maximum generation length of 32,768 tokens. GPT-5.6 Luna is evaluated through its API with reasoning effort medium, a limit of 32,768 completion tokens, and the provider’s default sampling parameters; its reasoning is not returned.

Fine-tuning of Qwen3-4B-Instruct.

The released Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 does not produce a reasoning block, so we fine-tune it on 1,000 Nemotron-3-30B-A3B traces before using it as a student (Section 4). Table 9 reports its scores before and after this step. The released model is evaluated with its plain prompt and no reasoning block; the fine-tuned model is the base model of the Qwen3-4B-Instruct block in Table 1.

Appendix B Prompt Templates

All prompts are given as the user message of the model’s chat template. For Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-1.7B, and Qwen3-0.6B, the student is prompted with the question:

Problem: {question xx}

Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}.

The self-teacher receives the same question together with the external teacher’s trace:

Problem: {question xx}

Here is a reference solution to this problem:

<reference_solution>
{trace zz}
</reference_solution>

After reading the reference solution above, make sure you truly understand the reasoning behind each step — do not copy or paraphrase it. Now, using your own words and independent reasoning, derive the same final answer to the problem above. Think step by step, explore different approaches, and don’t be afraid to backtrack or reconsider if something doesn’t work out:

Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}.

For Qwen3-4B-Instruct, the chat template opens the reasoning block (<think>) at the start of the response, and the last line of both prompts is additionally replaced by:

Think through the problem step by step inside <think> and </think> tags. After </think>, give your final solution and put the final answer within \boxed{}.

The token-level guidance is computed on the student’s original response tokens appended after each prompt; responses are not decoded and re-tokenized.

Teacher traces.

All three external teachers generate their traces from the same prompt:

Problem: {question xx}

Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}.

RLSD ablation.

For RLSD (Section 6.1), the self-teacher receives the ground-truth answer in place of the trace:

Problem: {question xx}

Here is a verified correct final answer to this problem:

<reference_solution>
{answer}
</reference_solution>

After reading the reference solution above, make sure you truly understand the reasoning behind each step — do not copy or paraphrase it. Now, using your own words and independent reasoning, derive the same final answer to the problem above. Think step by step, explore different approaches, and don’t be afraid to backtrack or reconsider if something doesn’t work out:

Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}.

Guide and hint ablations.

For the ablation on the form of the privileged context (Section 6.1), the external teacher rewrites its trace as a guide or as a hint. The guide is generated with:

You are helping a student who is stuck on a math problem. Below are the problem and a worked reasoning trace written by a stronger solver.

Problem:
{question xx}

Worked reasoning:
{trace zz}

Write a step-by-step guide for the student: a numbered list of the steps of the solution, in order, at most 8 steps and under 150 words in total. Rules: each step says what to do and why (the idea, the quantity to set up, the case split), without carrying out the computation; do not state the final answer; do not give intermediate numerical results; do not restate the problem; plain text, no markdown formatting. Output only the numbered list.

The hint is generated with the same opening, problem, and worked reasoning, followed by this instruction:

Write a hint of at most three sentences (under 80 words) that points the student to the key idea or the first decisive step. Rules: do not state the final answer; do not give numerical intermediate results; do not write out the solution; name the method or the observation that unlocks the problem. Output only the hint.

The self-teacher then receives the guide, with the verified final answer appended, in place of the reference solution:

Problem: {question xx}

Here is a step-by-step guide to this problem, followed by its verified final answer:

<guide>
{guide}
</guide>

After reading the guide above, make sure you truly understand why each step is needed — do not copy or paraphrase it. Now, using your own words and independent reasoning, carry out the steps and derive the same final answer to the problem above. Think step by step, explore different approaches, and don’t be afraid to backtrack or reconsider if something doesn’t work out:

Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}.

The self-teacher prompt for the hint is:

Problem: {question xx}

Here is a hint for this problem, followed by its verified final answer:

<hint>
{hint}
</hint>

After reading the hint above, make sure you truly understand the idea it points to — do not copy or paraphrase it. Now, using your own words and independent reasoning, work out the solution and derive the same final answer to the problem above. Think step by step, explore different approaches, and don’t be afraid to backtrack or reconsider if something doesn’t work out:

Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}.

Appendix C Proofs

Throughout, expectations are over prompts xx, traces zz, and rollouts y∼πθold(⋅∣x)y\sim\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(\cdot\mid x), where θold\theta_{\mathrm{old}} is the policy that sampled the rollouts and θ¯\bar{\theta} is the frozen copy of the student that serves as the self-teacher (Section 3.2), so that pt=πθold​(yt∣x,y<t)p_{t}=\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t}) and qt=πθ¯​(yt∣x,z,y<t)q_{t}=\pi_{\bar{\theta}}(y_{t}\mid x,z,y_{<t}) in Eq. 3; the response mask is left implicit. The quantities AA, δt\delta_{t}, and wtw_{t} carry no gradient, so the statements below do not depend on how often the self-teacher is synchronized.

C.1 Small-Gap Decomposition

Reverse-KL OPD trains the student with the token-level advantage A^tOPD=log⁡π∗​(yt∣st)−log⁡πθ​(yt∣st)\hat{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{OPD}}=\log\pi^{*}(y_{t}\mid s_{t})-\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid s_{t}), where π∗\pi^{*} is the teacher and st=(x,y<t)s_{t}=(x,y_{<t}); with a reference policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} it is equivalent to KL-regularized RL with the token reward rt=log⁡π∗​(yt∣st)−log⁡πref​(yt∣st)r_{t}=\log\pi^{*}(y_{t}\mid s_{t})-\allowbreak\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_{t}\mid s_{t}) (Agarwal et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026b). Taking the self-teacher as π∗\pi^{*} and the unconditioned student as πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} gives log⁡qt−log⁡pt\log q_{t}-\log p_{t}, whose stop-gradient value is δt\delta_{t}, so rtOPD,z=δtr_{t}^{\mathrm{OPD},z}=\delta_{t}. Writing Φλ,ϵ​(u)=(1−λ)+λ​clip1±ϵ⁡(e−u)\Phi_{\lambda,\epsilon}(u)=(1-\lambda)+\lambda\,\clip_{1\pm\epsilon}\!\left(e^{-u}\right), Eqs. 5 and 4 read

A~t=A⋅Φλ,ϵ(δt) 1{A<0}+A 1{A≥0},\tilde{A}_{t}\;=\;A\cdot\Phi_{\lambda,\epsilon}(\delta_{t})\,\mathbf{1}_{\{A<0\}}\;+\;A\,\mathbf{1}_{\{A\geq 0\}}, (6)

and since Φλ,ϵ>0\Phi_{\lambda,\epsilon}>0, sign⁡(A~t)=sign⁡(A)\sign(\tilde{A}_{t})=\sign(A), whereas the sign of A^tOPD\hat{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{OPD}} follows δt\delta_{t}.

Proposition 1 (Small-gap decomposition).

Ignoring clipping and evaluating the update at the policy that sampled the rollouts, θ=θold\theta=\theta_{\mathrm{old}}, for |δt|≪1|\delta_{t}|\ll 1 the BSD policy gradient satisfies

gBSD=gGRPO+O⁡(δt2)+λ𝔼[∑t𝟏{A<0}|A|δt∇θlogπθ(yt∣st)].g_{\mathrm{BSD}}\;=\;g_{\mathrm{GRPO}}\;+\;O(\delta_{t}^{2})\\ \;+\;\lambda\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\textstyle\sum_{t}\mathbf{1}_{\{A<0\}}\,|A|\;\delta_{t}\,\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid s_{t})\right]. (7)

This decomposition is an interpretation and does not guarantee stability or good credit assignment. It holds for any privileged context zz. With zz the ground-truth answer it describes the RLSD variant of Section 6.1, which also restricts the weight to unsuccessful rollouts; with a teacher trace, rtOPD,zr_{t}^{\mathrm{OPD},z} carries information from another model’s reasoning.

C.2 Proof of Proposition 1

The weight of Eq. 4 applies only to tokens with A<0A<0; tokens with A≥0A\geq 0 contribute their GRPO term unchanged. On A<0A<0 the BSD token advantage is

A~t=A⁡[(1−λ)+λ​e−δt],\tilde{A}_{t}=A\big[(1-\lambda)+\lambda e^{-\delta_{t}}\big], (8)

where clipping is ignored (it is inactive for |δt||\delta_{t}| small, since the clip interval [1−ϵ,1+ϵ][1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon] contains a neighborhood of 11). Expanding e−δt=1−δt+O⁡(δt2)e^{-\delta_{t}}=1-\delta_{t}+O(\delta_{t}^{2}) gives

A~t=A⁡[1−λ​δt]+O⁡(|A|​δt2)=A−λ​A​δt+O⁡(|A|​δt2).\begin{split}\tilde{A}_{t}&=A\big[1-\lambda\,\delta_{t}\big]+O\!\big(|A|\,\delta_{t}^{2}\big)\\ &=A-\lambda\,A\,\delta_{t}+O\!\big(|A|\,\delta_{t}^{2}\big).\end{split} (9)

Substituting into the policy gradient evaluated at the rollout policy, g=𝔼⁡[∑tA~t​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(yt∣st)]|θ=θoldg=\mathbb{E}[\sum_{t}\tilde{A}_{t}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid s_{t})]\big|_{\theta=\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}, where the PPO likelihood ratio equals one and its clipping is inactive, and writing −A=|A|-A=|A| on the reweighted tokens (A<0A<0) yields

gBSD=𝔼⁡[∑tA​∇θ​log⁡πθ]⏟gGRPO+O⁡(δt2)+λ𝔼[∑t𝟏{A<0}|A|δt∇θlogπθ].g_{\mathrm{BSD}}=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\Big[\textstyle\sum_{t}A\,\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}\Big]}_{g_{\mathrm{GRPO}}}+O(\delta_{t}^{2})\\ +\lambda\,\mathbb{E}\Big[\textstyle\sum_{t}\mathbf{1}_{\{A<0\}}\,|A|\,\delta_{t}\,\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}\Big]. (10)

Since δt=rtOPD,z\delta_{t}=r_{t}^{\mathrm{OPD},z}, the correction is an outcome-weighted OPD update restricted to unsuccessful rollouts. ∎

C.3 Weighting Successful Rollouts

Proposition 1 concerns unsuccessful rollouts only. Two different weights can be applied to rollouts with A>0A>0, and they act in opposite directions. The first is the weight of RLSD (Eq. 2), (1−λ)+λ​clip1±ϵ⁡(e+δt)(1-\lambda)+\lambda\,\clip_{1\pm\epsilon}\!\left(e^{+\delta_{t}}\right), which is the one used by the BSD (w/ succ.) variant of Section 6.1. Under the conditions of Proposition 1, it gives

A~t=A⁡[(1−λ)+λ​eδt]=A+λ​|A|​δt+O⁡(|A|​δt2),\begin{split}\tilde{A}_{t}&=A\big[(1-\lambda)+\lambda e^{\delta_{t}}\big]\\ &=A+\lambda\,|A|\,\delta_{t}+O\!\big(|A|\,\delta_{t}^{2}\big),\end{split} (11)

so the correction has the same form as on unsuccessful rollouts. The update of BSD (w/ succ.) is then the GRPO update plus an outcome-weighted OPD correction on all rollouts, which also pulls successful rollouts toward the self-teacher. The second applies the weight of Eq. 4, with e−δte^{-\delta_{t}}, unchanged to successful rollouts. It gives A~t=A−λ​|A|​δt+O⁡(|A|​δt2)\tilde{A}_{t}=A-\lambda\,|A|\,\delta_{t}+O(|A|\,\delta_{t}^{2}), whose correction has the opposite sign and pushes the policy away from the self-teacher on successful rollouts, rewarding divergence as in RLRT (Kim et al., 2026). We do not evaluate this second weight.

BSD uses neither weight. A successful rollout is a solution that the student found without the trace, and BSD reinforces it with its GRPO advantage alone, without moving it toward or away from the self-teacher. The expansion above describes what the first weight adds but does not by itself predict its effect on accuracy; the support for restricting the weight to unsuccessful rollouts is empirical, as BSD (w/ succ.) scores 61.4 against 63.9 for BSD (Section 6.1).

Appendix D Ablation Details

Table 11 gives the scores of Figure 4 on each benchmark, with the training step of each selected checkpoint and the magnitude of the mean token-level guidance of each form of context.

Training settings of the ablation variants.

GRPO, RLSD, and OPSD use the training problems, optimizer, learning rate, rollout budget (16 problems with 8 rollouts each), number of updates, and length limits of BSD (Table 4), and Table 10 lists where they differ. GRPO trains on the group-normalized verifier reward alone. RLSD applies the weight and schedule of BSD to unsuccessful rollouts, with a self-teacher that sees only the ground-truth answer. OPSD (Zhao et al., 2026) conditions a frozen copy of the base model on the full trace, following its original implementation, and uses the clipped log-probability difference between this self-teacher and the student as a token-level reward on every rollout, without the verifier reward. BSD-hint, BSD-guide, and BSD (w/ succ.) share the settings of BSD-trace except for the privileged context or, for BSD (w/ succ.), the weight on successful rollouts, which follows Eq. 2.

Figure 6 shows the mean response length of each variant on the three benchmarks at every saved checkpoint. The responses of OPSD shorten from 16.8k tokens at step 25 to 12.5k at step 150, against 17.5k for the base model, and its Avg@4 falls from 63.3 to 55.8 over the same steps. The other variants stay between 16.5k and 17.7k tokens.

Figure 7 gives an example in which the full trace provides more informative guidance than the answer. It shows the token-level guidance under the two forms of context on the same passage of an unsuccessful rollout of the Qwen3-4B student before training. In it the student computes the length of an interval incorrectly, writing 1/5m+11/5^{m+1} where the difference is 4/5m+14/5^{m+1}. With the full trace as context, which contains the correct derivation, the guidance is strongly negative on the incorrect numerator and on the tokens that carry the result into the next step. With the ground-truth answer as context, the guidance on the same tokens is close to zero, since the answer alone does not indicate which intermediate step is wrong.

Appendix E Wording of Incorrect and Correct Responses

The case study in Section 6.2 shows a single response. Here we compare the wording of responses across the three benchmarks, for the base Qwen3-4B and the student trained with BSD on Qwen3-32B traces, with four samples per problem from each model. On 26 problems the base model gives at least one incorrect response and the BSD student at least one correct response; these comprise 45 incorrect responses of the base model and 69 correct responses of the BSD student. For every word nn-gram with n≤3n\leq 3 that is frequent in these responses (1,508 nn-grams), we compute its rate per 1,000 words in the two groups for each problem and a paired tt-statistic over the problems. The rates of 24 nn-grams differ with |t|>3|t|>3, where about four are expected by chance; Table 12 lists examples. Incorrect responses of the base model contain more expressions of negation and doubt, and correct responses of the BSD student more expressions of verification. The correct responses are also shorter, with 19,057 tokens on average against 24,279. This comparison changes the model and the correctness of the response at the same time, so the differences cannot be attributed to BSD alone. We report them as a description of the two groups of responses and not as independent evidence that BSD induces self-correction.

Appendix I Out-of-Domain Evaluation

To examine how the distillation methods affect out-of-domain performance, we evaluate the Qwen3-4B student on general knowledge and legal questions, at every saved checkpoint of BSD, SFT, and the OPD variant of each teacher. We use two sets of 200 multiple-choice questions: from MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024), 20 questions from each of its ten categories other than mathematics, physics, chemistry, and engineering, and from LEXam (Fan et al., 2026), 200 four-choice questions in English and German, sampled in the proportion of the two languages in the benchmark. The protocol is that of Table 7, and the base model scores 63.5 on the MMLU-Pro questions and 45.9 on the LEXam questions.

Figure 9 shows that SFT is unstable during training, whereas BSD and the OPD variants are not. On the MMLU-Pro questions, SFT with GPT-5.6 Luna falls steadily from 62.1 at step 25 to 54.1 at step 150, 9.4 points below the base model, and SFT with Nemotron-3-30B-A3B falls from 64.0 to 60.8. On the LEXam questions, SFT with GPT-5.6 falls to 40.5 at step 100, 5.4 points below the base model. Under a bootstrap paired over questions, these three differences from the base model exclude zero at the 95% level, whereas no difference of SFT with Qwen3-32B does. In contrast, at every checkpoint and for all three teachers, BSD and the OPD variants are never more than 1.1 points below the base model on the MMLU-Pro questions and 3.5 points on the LEXam questions. Learning from the student’s own rollouts therefore preserves its abilities outside the training domain, whereas imitating the teacher’s reasoning traces can erase them.

Figure 10 shows the mean response length in the same evaluations. With GPT-5.6 Luna, SFT shortens the responses from 3,031 to 1,059 tokens on the MMLU-Pro questions and from 4,255 to 1,975 tokens on the LEXam questions, against 3,159 and 4,302 tokens for the base model, and with Nemotron-3-30B-A3B it lengthens them to 3,600 tokens on the MMLU-Pro questions. BSD and the OPD variants stay within 300 tokens of the base model at every checkpoint. The loss of out-of-domain accuracy under SFT thus coincides with the change in response length that it shows on mathematics (Section 5.2).

Table 15 summarizes each run by the mean and standard deviation of its score over the six checkpoints. BSD averages 63.8 to 64.5 on the MMLU-Pro questions and 43.9 to 44.9 on the LEXam questions, with a standard deviation of at most 1.1 points, and the OPD variants behave similarly. SFT with GPT-5.6 Luna averages 59.6 on the MMLU-Pro questions with a standard deviation of 3.1 points. The base model has a single checkpoint, so we report its standard deviation over the four sampling seeds; on the LEXam questions it is 4.9 points, and the gap between the base model and the trained students there is comparable to this sampling noise.
